stem: Environmental services is prioritizing cleaning in a patient-care room with frequent staff contact. Which surfaces should receive particular attention as frequently touched surfaces?

options.A: Bed rails, bedside tables, call controls, doorknobs, commodes, and nearby patient-care equipment.
options.B: Ceiling tiles, upper wall surfaces, and other areas with minimal routine hand contact.
options.C: Floors and distant wall surfaces before bed rails and bedside controls because low-touch surfaces should be prioritized first.
options.D: Windows and other minimally touched surfaces while delaying cleaning of nearby patient-contact surfaces.

rationale: CDC isolation-precautions guidance states that cleaning and disinfection should emphasize frequently touched surfaces, especially those closest to the patient and most likely to be contaminated. Examples include bed rails, bedside tables, commodes, doorknobs, sinks, and surfaces or equipment in close proximity to the patient. CDC environmental guidance separately distinguishes these high-touch surfaces from minimal-hand-contact surfaces such as floors and ceilings, which do not receive the same cleaning priority based on touch frequency.
educational_objective: Prioritize frequently touched surfaces near the patient for environmental cleaning and disinfection rather than low-touch environmental surfaces.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: II. Fundamental Elements Needed to Prevent Transmission of Infectious Agents in Healthcare Settings
source_locator: Section II.I. Environmental Measures, especially paragraph identifying frequently touched surfaces closest to the patient; supporting Environmental Services guidance distinguishing frequent- from minimal-hand-contact surfaces.
source_claim_supported: CDC states that frequently touched surfaces, especially those closest to the patient, should receive particular cleaning/disinfection attention and lists bedrails, bedside tables, commodes, doorknobs, sinks, and nearby surfaces/equipment as examples.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Appendix A, printed p. 26, Safety and Infection Prevention and Control → Standard Precautions/Transmission-Based Precautions/Surgical Asepsis: apply principles of infection prevention and evaluate adherence to aseptic/infection-control practices.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — environmental infection prevention

source_original.stem: Environmental services is prioritizing cleaning in a room occupied by a client with frequent staff contact. Which surfaces should receive particular attention as high-touch surfaces?

options.A: Bed rails, bedside tables, call controls, doorknobs, commodes, and nearby equipment.
options.B: Ceiling tiles, upper wall corners, and light fixtures.
options.C: Prioritize floors and lower wall surfaces because they accumulate the greatest environmental bioburden during routine care.
options.D: Windows and ceiling vents unless blood or body fluid is visible.

source_original.rationale: Frequently touched surfaces close to the patient accumulate repeated hand contact and are more likely to participate in contact transmission. CDC specifically highlights bedrails, bedside tables, commodes, doorknobs, sinks, and nearby equipment for appropriate routine cleaning and disinfection.
source_original.source_detail: CDC Isolation Precautions — Environmental Measures: prioritize cleaning/disinfection of frequently touched surfaces near the patient such as bedrails, bedside tables, commodes, doorknobs and nearby equipment. Current CDC isolation-precautions guidance at exact URL; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control; Reporting of Incident/Event and infection/safety activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the high-touch-surface construct and key. Removed unsupported claims about 'greatest environmental bioburden' and a blood/body-fluid exception, and rewrote distractors around the CDC-supported distinction between frequently touched near-patient surfaces and minimal-touch surfaces. Updated the exact CDC page date and locator.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Environmental infection prevention — high-touch surface cleaning
audit_findings.exact_locator: II.I Environmental Measures directly lists frequently touched near-patient examples; CDC Environmental Services supports the high-touch/minimal-touch distinction.
audit_findings.claim_audit: All final claims are bounded to touch frequency/proximity and CDC examples; no unsupported bioburden ranking or special contamination exception remains.

distractor_audit.A: Directly matches CDC examples and priority principle.
distractor_audit.B: Contains surfaces CDC classifies as minimal hand-contact rather than high-touch priorities.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrectly reverses the CDC high-touch priority.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrectly delays near-patient high-touch cleaning in favor of minimal-touch surfaces.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A consists of routinely high-touch near-patient surfaces.
audit_findings.cueing: All options compare environmental surface groups; the key requires recognizing touch-frequency risk, not spotting an absurd mechanism.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN 2026 Safety and Infection Prevention and Control covers infection-prevention practices in care environments.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Adversarial reread verified examples and avoided claims that all floors or windows are never clinically relevant; the item asks only which group deserves particular high-touch attention.
